title: What Keeps It Standing
logline: A fifty-foot footbridge of timber over a hill stream, roofed and tiled for its whole length, in which the planks, the posts, the rails and the pegs that fasten them are all the same material — so that the thing holding it up and the thing being held are not two different things — and whose own age nobody can establish.
human_question: If I cannot find out what made something, can I still find out what is holding it?

place.what_kind_of_place: One small roofed footbridge over a rocky hill stream in closed forest, with a rock-cave temple standing beside it and a village footpath running across it. It is about fifty feet from end to end and narrow enough that two people pass each other carefully, and it is covered for its entire span by a tiled roof at about the height of a raised hand, so that crossing it is walking through a low wooden corridor rather than over open water. The decking, the beams, the posts standing in the stream bed, the handrails, the carved rafter laths and the pins that fasten all of it are described as timber throughout. It is a protected monument, it is fragile, and it is in daily use by the people who live on the path.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: It is the opposite of a view. Everything the film wants is inside a space the size of a corridor: bars of daylight coming through the gaps between roof tiles and lying across dry planks, the same planks with moving water showing through their joints, the deep grain of a beam a hand's width from the lens, a halved joint where two members cross, and a wooden peg driven through both and worn flush with the surface. Under it the stream goes over rock loudly enough to be the whole soundtrack, and the air inside smells of old timber and river at once. The payoff is not a wide shot. It is a peg the size of a finger, held long enough that the viewer understands it is carrying the bridge.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, and that is the point. The water moves. The light through the roof gaps moves across the deck through the middle of the day and then goes out. Somebody crosses, at their own pace, and the boards take their weight and say so. The stream changes scale across the year — thin and clear in the dry months, heavy and brown and carrying rock after the north-east monsoon, which is the load the structure has survived four hundred-odd times or two hundred or eight hundred, depending on which account is believed.
place.when_it_looks_best: Two separate windows, both on the ground, both in available light. Around the middle of a clear day for the bars of light through the tile gaps, which are the only lighting the interior will ever have. Then the last half hour before dark for the film's dimmest sustained frame, when the roof gaps go dull and the water underneath is heard rather than seen. Dry months for safe access to the stream bed and the underside; the weeks after the north-east monsoon for the loudest water and the highest flow, filmed from the bank only.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: The smallest, closest, darkest film in its group and the only interior one. There is no drone, no horizon, no weather event and almost no camera movement: a descent through trees on a hundred rough steps, a timber corridor over loud water, and then a long look at how it is made — grain, joints, worn boards, a peg. It resolves on its own terms, from the outside in and from the whole span down to one fastening, and it ends on an object the size of a hand. Someone with no interest in philosophy gets a complete, quiet piece about how a wooden thing stands up.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the plainest possible demonstration of a technical point the sources make twice and that almost everybody who quotes them gets wrong. When these texts call greed, hatred, confusion and their three opposites 'roots', they say explicitly that they do not mean causes of arising. They mean what a state of mind stands on — a root is what keeps a tree from falling, not why it grew. This is a structure whose support is the same material as the thing supported, fastened with pins of its own substance, and it is also a structure whose origin the record has genuinely lost. So the film can hold the two questions apart in front of the viewer: what made this is unknown and may stay unknown, and what is holding it is under your feet and can be photographed. The voice never claims the second explains the first.

sequence.on_screen: Late afternoon under closed canopy. Handheld, following about a hundred rough steps down through trees towards a sound of water that arrives well before the water does. At the bottom the span appears end-on: a low timber corridor with a tiled roof, going out over the stream and stopping.
sequence.voice: The texts this film is reading list six things they call roots. Greed, hatred and confusion, and then the three opposites of those. And both of them say, early and flatly, that they are not called roots because they make a state of mind happen. One of them stops to say it in so many words: this is not the sense in which fire causes smoke.

sequence.on_screen: Inside the span, camera set low on the deck, available light only, no movement. Thin bars of daylight through the gaps between roof tiles lying across the planks; in the joints between the planks, moving water. Nobody in frame.
sequence.voice: The picture they use instead is a tree. Roots are not the reason a tree grew. They are the reason it is not lying down. A root, in this sense, is what holds a state of mind onto the thing it has taken hold of, the way roots keep a tree standing. Which changes the question. Not what started this. What is holding it.

sequence.on_screen: Macro on a tripod in the dimmest part of the span. The end grain of a beam. A halved joint where two members cross. A wooden peg about the length of a finger, driven through both and worn flush with the surface. Then wider, from the bank: a round post standing in the stream bed with the whole span coming down onto it.
sequence.voice: So look at what is actually here. Planks onto beams, beams onto posts, posts into the river bed. And the pins holding it all together are cut from the same wood as the parts they are holding. There is no second material in here doing the work of support. Whatever keeps this up, it is made of the same stuff as the thing being kept up.

sequence.on_screen: The foot of a post where it meets the stream bed, filmed from the bank at the water's level: whatever is actually there — bare timber set into rock, or the collar of grey concrete that some accounts say was poured round it — weathered, mossy, visibly a different age from everything above it. Water running past.
sequence.voice: How old is it, then. The sentence you will hear most often is that it was built in the sixteenth century, in the time of the kingdom of Dambadeniya. But Dambadeniya's kings ruled in the twelve hundreds. That sentence puts one bridge in two centuries three hundred years apart, and it is the sentence almost everyone repeats. The others say four hundred years, or six hundred, or eight hundred. The only reason ever offered for any of them is that the carving looks like Kandyan work.

sequence.on_screen: Long lens from the far bank through leaves: the whole span in profile, dark inside, and one adult crossing it end to end at their own pace, far enough off and low enough in the frame that they are not identifiable. The stream loud over rock below them.
sequence.voice: It would be easy, and wrong, to call that confusion. These texts are careful at exactly this point. The doubt they treat as a fault is not the ordinary state of not knowing something you have no way of settling, and one of them says so outright. Nobody who has crossed this needed the century. What was under them did not depend on it.

sequence.on_screen: The film's dimmest sustained frame. The interior at the end of the light: roof gaps gone dull, the deck nearly black, the water beneath heard and barely seen. The camera does not move and nothing enters the shot.
sequence.voice: What they do say about confusion is narrower and stranger than a hidden mechanism waiting to be exposed. They call it a darkening, a thing that stops a matter being known as it is. It lies under every harmful state they list, and in two of them it is the only root present. Those two are the flattest states in the whole scheme. They carry no pleasure and no pain, because what has not been taken hold of can be neither enjoyed nor resented. That is not calm. It is just grey.

sequence.on_screen: Back on the peg, hand-sized in frame, held. A thumb's width of wood, dry, flush with the beam, the grain of the beam running past it the other way. Held until the light goes off it.
sequence.voice: Six roots on one list, and every item on it is the same kind of item. Three hold a mind onto what it wants, or onto what it will not forgive, or onto not seeing. Three hold it the other way: letting go, goodwill, and understanding. One of the texts says the second three are the stronger, and it means something narrow by that — each of them undoes its own opposite, one for one. Not a better material fetched in from somewhere else. The same substance, turned round.

concept_merge.why_together: C033 is the film and C008 is the correction that keeps it honest. Read fresh, C033's whole interest is a definition almost nobody preserves in quotation: there are six roots, greed, hatred and delusion and their opposites [C033-P:L29; C033-M:L3], and both sources go out of their way to deny that they are called roots because they cause a mind to arise [C033-P:L81; C033-M:L5]. Pradeepika even names the actual conditions of arising separately, so that the roots are left doing one job only [C033-P:L81], and Margaya contrasts the Abhidhamma sense of the word with the everyday sense in which fire causes smoke [C033-M:L5]. What a root does instead is hold: it fixes the mind and its companions firmly on their object, as a tree's roots keep the tree standing [C033-P:L27; C033-M:L5–L7], and Pradeepika extends the same image to roots drawing up what eventually becomes fruit [C033-P:L79]. That is a structural claim, not a causal one, and it wants a structure rather than a process on screen. C008 then supplies what C033's own digest says it cannot supply on its own: C033 nowhere states in a single sentence that delusion underlies every unwholesome state — that is an inference from its tables [C033-P:L45; C033-P:L53–L54] — and the direct statement is in C008, where delusion is defined as a darkening that prevents a matter being known as it is, present in all unwholesome minds and dominant in two [C008-M:L3]. Those two are the one-rooted minds of C033's arithmetic [C033-P:L39–L65; C033-M:L9–L13], and C008 describes them from the inside: always neutral in feeling, because what has not been grasped can be neither enjoyed nor disliked [C008-P:L25–L30; C008-P:L30], and arising unprompted [C008-P:L70].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That 'what made this?' and 'what is holding this up?' are two different questions, and that a place can answer the second while permanently withholding the first. C033 alone, on a building, would slide into the modern sense of 'root cause' that its own digest forbids [C033-M:L5; C033-P:L81]. C008 alone would make the film a study of a confused record. Together they produce the film's one move: the structure is visible and can be put a hand on, the origin is not, and the sources are talking about the first kind of thing. C008 also polices the film's second temptation. The honest answer to the bridge's age is that nobody consulted knows, and it would be cheap to call that doubt — Pradeepika explicitly excludes ordinary not-knowing about what one cannot yet investigate from the doubt it treats as a hindrance [C008-P:L36], and restricts that doubt to eight specific matters [C008-P:L38–L58]. So the film says the contradiction out loud and then declines to diagnose it, which is the only use of C008 the digest actually licenses. The pairing finally closes off the metaphor: because the six roots are one list of one kind of item, three that grip and three that free [C033-P:L29], and because Pradeepika's claim that the wholesome ones are stronger is the narrow claim that each undoes its own opposite [C033-P:L83], the closing shot of a wooden pin in a wooden beam is not a symbol of a hidden mechanism. It is the same category twice: the fastening is not a foreign material.

concept_links.why: The concept is six roots — greed, hatred and delusion and their three opposites [C033-P:L29; C033-M:L3] — and its whole weight is on what 'root' means. Both sources deny that they are causes of a mind's arising [C033-P:L81; C033-M:L5]; what they do is hold the mind and its companions firmly on their object, as a tree's roots keep it standing [C033-P:L27; C033-M:L5–L7], and Pradeepika carries the image on to roots drawing up what becomes fruit [C033-P:L79]. This location is a structure in which the holding and the held are the same material: decking, beams, posts, rails and the pins that fasten them are all described as timber, so support is not something added from a second substance. The arithmetic belongs here too — 18 rootless minds, 71 rooted, 2 with a single root, 22 with two and 47 with all three wholesome ones [C033-P:L39–L65; C033-M:L9–L13] — because unwholesome minds never carry three [C033-P:L45; C033-P:L53–L54] and no mind carries only one wholesome root [C033-M:L11], and the film's last beat is the list as a list. The digest's limits are load-bearing and are written into the risks rather than softened: this is not root-cause analysis and the film may never say greed is the root cause of anything [C033-M:L5; C033-P:L81]; non-delusion is not education, information or expertise but the wisdom factor inside a moment of mind [C033-M:L3], which matters acutely in a film about a record nobody has established, because the voice must not imply that better research would be amoha; the roots classify moments of mind and not persons, so nobody crossing the bridge is a type; and Pradeepika's claim that the wholesome roots are stronger [C033-P:L83] is the narrow claim that each undoes its specific opposite, not a message that good outweighs bad.

C008 supplies three things C033's digest says C033 cannot. First, the direct statement that delusion is a darkening which prevents a matter being known as it is, present in all unwholesome minds and dominant in two [C008-M:L3]; C033's own uncertainties note that its version of this is an inference from tables and that the plain sentence is here. Second, the interior of the two one-rooted minds: doubt and restlessness, both always accompanied by neutral feeling because a mind that cannot grasp its object can neither enjoy nor dislike it [C008-P:L25–L30; C008-M:L7–L9; C008-P:L30], both arising unprompted [C008-P:L70], restlessness being the loss of the power to stay with one object, which sends the rest of the mind astray [C008-P:L62–L64]. Third, and most importantly for this film, the limit. The received account of this bridge contradicts itself and the honest answer about its age is that nobody knows — and the digest forbids calling that the doubt it warns about, since Pradeepika expressly separates ordinary not-knowing about something one cannot yet investigate from the hindrance [C008-P:L36] and restricts the hindrance to eight named matters [C008-P:L38–L58]. So the film states the contradiction and refuses the diagnosis, in the voice, on screen. The other does_not_transfer lines are live too and are in the risks: the neutral feeling of these states is not equanimity, which is a real danger in a film whose most beautiful frame is a dim quiet interior; restlessness is not a productivity problem [C008-P:L62]; the concept is not an argument against questioning [C008-P:L36] and equally not a slogan for scepticism, Margaya's remedy being devotional confidence [C008-M:L18]; and 'weak' does not mean harmless, since doubt still turns the mind from good and weakens the good done with it [C008-M:L16].

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the word 'root', in these texts, does not mean cause. It means whatever a thing is standing on right now — which is a question you can ask about this minute rather than about your history, and which has an answer even when the history has been lost. The structure on screen makes the distinction without any help: nobody can tell you what year it was built, and anybody can put a hand on what is holding it up.
what_must_be_real: Nothing on this structure is touched, tested, leaned on, loaded, weighted, prised, sampled or dismantled for the camera, and no member, peg, tile or rail is moved to get a better angle. No part of it is lit artificially at any point: the interior is filmed on daylight through the roof gaps and on whatever is left at the end of the day, and if a frame cannot be exposed without adding light the frame is lost rather than lit. No crew weight beyond one person and a tripod is on the deck at a time, no tripod foot goes on a joint or a rail, and nothing is set down on the boards that is not carried off again. The stream bed and the bank are where the underside is filmed from, not the underside itself. Written permission from the Department of Archaeology is obtained before any filming, and the temple's own consent before anything on temple ground; the bridge, the cave temple and the monks' dwelling are all protected monuments and are treated as such. If the temple is in use, no act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repositioned or lit, and no observance is filmed as material. Nobody in frame is an exhibit: a person crossing is a person crossing, never an illustration of a state of mind, and no shot presents anyone as confused, hesitant, doubting or lost. Anyone identifiable has agreed, in their own language, in a situation where refusing costs them nothing; on a village path that means asking before filming and accepting no, every time. Children are not filmed using the bridge or anywhere else on this location, and if children are on the span the camera does not roll — this is a footpath to a village and a temple and it is planned for rather than hoped about. The condition of the structure is filmed as it is: if conservation has added iron, cement, concrete abutments or replacement timber, those appear in the film and the voice says they are there, because the received sentence about this bridge is that it contains no metal at all and the film does not protect that sentence. The dating is left unsettled on screen exactly as it is unsettled in the record; no century is asserted, no caption or lower third supplies one, and the impossible formula is quoted as a formula rather than corrected into a rival date.
position_hint: Late in the group's middle, and deliberately after the wide, weather-driven films: it is the moment the group stops looking for the way out of the fog and asks what anything is resting on. It is also the group's smallest and quietest film and works best between two large ones. Nothing in the placement depends on the location.
risks: The metaphor lecture. 'You cannot see what holds it up, and neither can you see delusion' is the sentence this film must not contain. The digests license no reading of delusion as a concealed mechanism that could be exposed, and the structure's point is the opposite anyway: here you can see what holds it up. The voice says what the structure is, says what the sources mean by a root, and does not weld the two with a flourish.

Saying 'root cause'. Both sources explicitly deny that these roots cause a mind to arise [C033-M:L5; C033-P:L81], and the everyday phrase would misstate the concept in a film whose whole subject is that definition. It must not appear in the narration, in a caption, or in the way a beat is framed.

Implying that non-delusion is research, expertise or better information. The digest is explicit that amoha is the wisdom factor within a moment of mind and not education or IQ [C033-M:L3]. A film built on a record nobody has established is one step from 'if only the archaeology were better', which would be a different and wrong claim.

Selling the dark interior as serenity. The film's most beautiful frame is a dim, quiet, enclosed space, and beat 6 describes states the sources call flat and neutral. C008's digest states plainly that this neutral feeling is not equanimity or calm and that presenting a dull undecided mood as serene reverses the source. The voice names it as grey, and the grade must not make the frame devotional.

Diagnosing the record. Calling the contradictory dating an instance of vicikicchā would break the digest's own separation of ordinary not-knowing from the hindrance [C008-P:L36] and its restriction of the hindrance to eight named matters [C008-P:L38–L58]. The film reports the contradiction and stops.

Reading the film as a lament for a lost craft, or as national pride in ancient carpentry. Nearly every popular account of this bridge ends in exactly that register, and C061's bar on legacy and remembrance framing is live. This is not a film about what has been forgotten, what was better once, or what should be recovered. No king, kingdom or craft tradition is narrated as glorious and no skill is mourned.

Drawing this sense of 'root' together with the root-condition of the conditional-relations teaching. C033's digest states that neither extract covers the relation and that it needs expert checking before any film joins them. The film does not go near it.

Presenting the wholesome roots as 'positivity wins'. Pradeepika's strength claim is specific — each wholesome root undoes its own opposite, and results are suppressed [C033-P:L83]. Beat 7 is written to keep it that narrow and can still drift in delivery.

Treating the people who use the path as material. This is a working footpath; a shot of somebody crossing is very easy to cut as an illustration of hesitation or of not knowing. It is not one, and the sources' roots classify moments of mind rather than persons.

Children. The bridge is on a village path to a temple and school-age children will cross it. There is no version of this film in which a child appears, and the shooting plan has to schedule around the times they use it rather than rely on luck.

The structure itself. It is small, old, timber, protected, and under a stream that carries rock in the monsoon. A crew that behaves as if it were robust is the real hazard here, more than any doctrinal error.

Discovering that the purity claim is false. If conservation has put iron nails, cement or concrete abutments into it, the 'nothing but wood' sentence in beats 3 and 7 has to be rewritten on site to describe what is actually there. The film survives that — the argument is about support being the same substance as the thing supported, which the original joinery still shows — but the narration cannot be recorded before the structure is inspected.

Drone use. Almost certainly the wrong tool: a fifty-foot roofed span under closed canopy over a narrow gorge does not read from the air, an aerial would show trees and a roof, and the noise and downwash near a protected timber structure and a temple are an additional reason not to. The film is built entirely from the ground and the shot list contains no aerial.
drop_if: The Department of Archaeology, or the temple, declines filming, or permits it only on conditions that would mean touching, loading or lighting the structure.
The structure cannot be filmed without crew weight or equipment on it beyond one person and a tripod, or the deck is in a condition where even that is unwise.
The interior cannot be exposed on available light at any hour, so that the film's central frames would need artificial light.
The underside, the posts and the joints cannot be reached and framed from the bank or the stream bed, which would remove the macro payoff and with it the film's ending.
Conservation has replaced enough of the fabric that the timber-on-timber joinery and the wooden pins are no longer visible anywhere on the structure. The argument needs one real joint in shot.
Filming cannot be scheduled so that no child is on the span while the camera rolls.

The dating turns out to be settled after all by a source this desk research missed — a dated inscription, a grant, a radiocarbon or tree-ring result. Beats 4 and 5 are then wrong, and the film is rebuilt rather than kept with the contradiction it no longer has.

connections.note: Explicit separation, because the two could be confused and must not be. IDEA-0054 is about routes: a wetland crossed by three incompatible ideas of how to get through it, and the not-knowing there is about which way to go. This film contains no question about ways through. Its bridge is not a choice, a route or a crossing-as-decision; it is a structure, and the only question asked of it is what it is standing on. Nothing in this film compares the path over it with any other path, and nobody in it is deciding anything. If a cut or a narration line in either film starts to make the other's argument, this one gives way: C033's root is not a direction.
Two films about being held rather than being caused: a circle in stubble exactly as wide as a rope is long, and a span held up by pins of its own wood.
Both films are about foundations and what the record has lost, and they are shot as opposites: an emptied reservoir basin, wide and bare and bright, against fifty feet of dark timber interior.

selection.reason: It is the group's only treatment of the six roots as a list, including the wholesome three, and after the rewrite it is the only film in the group whose philosophy is carried by a built structure and a documentary contradiction rather than by resemblance to a landscape. It is also the group's only enclosed, close, dark, drone-free film, which is what the differentiation rule asks of it.

review.note: Rewritten in full on 2026-09-25 and the verdict reset; the previous body — a mangrove channel network in a lagoon behind a sand bar — is gone, along with its location. It went for two reasons. First, monoculture: nine of this group's eleven films carried the philosophy by analogy at a working or natural place, and the mangrove film was among the purest examples, a landscape that happened to resemble what C033 says about roots, with no story on it that asked C033's question. Second, overlap: IDEA-0054 in this same group is already a film about incompatible channels through a coastal wetland, so two of eleven films were branching water in mangrove and reed, and the weaker one had to go. The replacement is bound to a historical structure instead of a resemblance — the oldest surviving wooden bridge in the country by the received account, on an ancient footpath route between two royal capitals, every component including its nails described as timber, and an age that the record cannot settle: the most repeated sentence about it puts its construction in the sixteenth century during the Dambadeniya era, and Dambadeniya was a thirteenth-century capital, so the sentence is internally impossible, while rival accounts give four hundred, six hundred, eight hundred years, the last king of Kandy and an eighteenth-century king. That contradiction is spelled out in what_is_disputed rather than smoothed, along with a second finding the research turned up: several accounts say concrete was laid round the posts in 1986 and that iron nails and concrete abutments have since been added, which puts the 'nothing but wood' formula itself in question and is now something the film must check on site and show. The treatment is also new and is the group's smallest and darkest: no drone at all, one structure, an interior of timber under tile with light through the gaps, water underneath, macro on joinery, and a payoff the size of a hand. Both digests were re-read fresh, every citation re-resolved against their own evidence, and the film's use of C008 was narrowed to what the digest licenses — the record's unsettledness is reported and explicitly not diagnosed as the doubt the sources warn about. An explicit connections entry records the separation from IDEA-0054.

suggested_location.name: The Bogoda wooden bridge and Bogoda Raja Maha Viharaya, over the Gallanda Oya
suggested_location.region: Badulla District, Uva Province: Bogoda village in Grama Niladhari Division No. 76 of Bogoda, Haliela Divisional Secretariat, in hill country west of Badulla town, reached from the Hali Ela junction on the Badulla–Bandarawela road.
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place found that puts the concept's exact definition and the film's whole visual argument inside one object. C033's roots are not causes; they are what a state stands on, and the sources' own image for it is a tree's roots keeping a tree upright. This is a structure with nothing in it but itself: the decking, the beams, the posts in the stream bed, the handrails, the carved rafter laths and the pins that fasten them are all described as timber, so the thing holding it up is the same material as the thing being held. Four centuries of people, or two, or eight, have walked over a span whose support they could not identify by looking at it, and could have put a hand on at any time. And the second concept is supplied by the record rather than staged: the single most repeated sentence about this bridge is internally impossible, and the honest answer to how old it is, after reading everything findable, is that nobody consulted knows. It is also the right scale for the group's missing treatment — one interior, one lens length, no aerial, no weather, no crowd — and the payoff is a wooden peg.
what_to_film: The descent: about a hundred rough steps down through trees, handheld, with the stream arriving on the soundtrack before it is in frame, and the span appearing end-on at the bottom.

The interior from the deck, on a low tripod, in available light only: bars of daylight through the gaps between roof tiles lying across the planks, and moving water visible in the joints between the same planks.

Macro on the joinery, which is the film's argument and its ending: end grain, a halved joint where two members cross, the carved rafter laths, and above all a wooden pin driven through a joint and worn flush with the surface, framed hand-sized.

The posts and the underside, filmed from the bank and the stream bed and never from on or under the structure: the round columns standing in the rock, the central pier, and whatever is actually at the foot of a post — bare timber, or the concrete some accounts say was poured round it in 1986.
One adult crossing, on a long lens from the far bank, distant and unidentifiable, filmed only with consent and never framed as an illustration of a state of mind. No children, at any distance.
The stream itself at two flows if the schedule allows: thin and clear in the dry months, heavy after the north-east monsoon, both from the bank.
The dimmest sustained frame the interior will give at the end of the day, static, with the water heard rather than seen. This is beat 6 and it is the film's darkest point.

Sound, deliberately and separately: water over rock under a timber deck, boards under a foot, rain on tiles a few feet above the head, and the particular quiet of a roofed span between two loud banks.
suggested_location.access: The road access is from the Hali Ela junction on the Badulla–Bandarawela road, marked by a small signboard; about 11 km on the Hali Ela–Welimada road to Jangulla junction, then left about 2.5 km, the road narrow but motorable and ending at the temple. A second route, via Meegahakiula and the Alugolla road and then the Kandegedara school road, is given as 23.3 km. From the end of the road, about a hundred steps descend to the river; the bridge and the cave temple are both at the bottom. Distances quoted for the site vary widely and inconsistently — 7 km west of Badulla, 13 km south of Badulla, 10 km, 11 km from Hali Ela, 15 km from Ella — and the coordinates put it roughly 7 km west-north-west of the town in a straight line, with the larger figures being road distances by different routes. The bridge, the cave temple and the monks' dwelling are gazetted archaeological protected monuments, and the site is a temple in use on a village footpath, so both the Department of Archaeology and the temple have to be approached before filming. Nothing about access, permission or conditions has been verified.
suggested_location.best_time: Two windows, both on foot and both in available light. The middle of a clear day for the bars of light through the roof gaps, which are the only interior lighting that will ever exist; the last half hour of light for the film's darkest frame. Seasonally, the driest stretch in this part of the hill country is around June and July, which is when the stream is lowest and the bank and bed are safe to work from; October and November are the wettest months and the north-east monsoon through to about January puts the most water and the most rock down the stream, which is the load the structure has survived and worth filming from the bank. Avoid the temple's own busy days for anything on temple ground.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search, done on 25 September 2026. Nothing has been seen on the ground, no permission has been sought, and no printed source was read. The scholarly spine of the site description comes from one page, lankapradeepa.com, which cites three works this research could not obtain: Lalchandra 1993 for the measurements, the construction and most of the temple description; Paranavitana 1970 for the Brahmi inscription and its translation; and Priyadarshani and Gunasena 2017, the Department of Archaeology's Badulla district inventory. Every figure attributed to those works here is therefore reported at one remove and should be checked against the printed texts before anything is filmed or narrated. Coordinates are the OpenStreetMap node for the bridge, retrieved through Nominatim, and were not checked against a survey sheet; they place the site about 7 km west-north-west of Badulla in a straight line, which is consistent with the English Wikipedia's '7 kilometres west' and not with the widely repeated '13 km south', a figure that appears to be road distance. Access directions come from amazinglanka.com and from a 2016 Roar Sinhala article and are unverified. The 1986 concrete claim reaches this research only through search indexing of the Serendib magazine article 'The Wooden Bridge of Bogoda'; the article's own host was unreachable at the time of writing and the sentence could not be read in place, so it is held as a reported claim and not as fact. The claims that iron nails and concrete support beams have been added, and that the span now stands on concrete abutments replacing the original wooden pillars, come from travel pages with no source attached and cannot all be true alongside each other or alongside Lalchandra's description of round wooden columns. A first restoration in 1963–64 surfaced in a search summary attributed to Sinhala Wikipedia but is not in that article's wikitext as read here and no source for it was found; it is not used. The dating was pursued specifically and nothing was settled: no inscription, chronicle entry, land grant, radiocarbon date or tree-ring study for the bridge's own timber was located, and every date found rests on stylistic comparison with Kandyan-period work. The Sinhala Wikipedia article carries an unanswered citation-needed tag dated September 2010 on 'the oldest wooden bridge' and another dated December 2011 on 'built from a single tree'. Species names were cross-read between the English and Sinhala Wikipedia articles and the Roar article, which disagree on how many species were used. The five Commons images were all confirmed to exist through action=query&titles= before their URLs were written; three are listed as CC BY-SA 4.0 and two as CC BY-SA 3.0, and two of the five are small files. No image of the joinery or of a wooden pin was found on Commons, which is the film's payoff shot and exists here only as a research direction.

historical_thread.story:
The structure is a covered footbridge of timber over a rocky hill stream, standing beside a rock-cave temple in a village at the end of a road that goes no further. It crosses the Gallanda Oya, a tributary of the Mahaweli, and it is described in every account as the only surviving wooden bridge of its kind in the country and, in most of them, as the oldest surviving wooden bridge in Sri Lanka. What makes it unusual is not the span but two other things: it is roofed and tiled along its entire length, with flat tiles of the kind used in the Kandyan period, so that crossing it means walking through a low wooden corridor; and every component of it is said to be timber, including the pins that fasten the parts together. The archaeological description lists the decking, the roof, the roof tiles, the balustrades and the nails as all being made of wood.

The only measured description of it found in this research is M.D. Lalchandra's, in a paper titled 'Bridges in ancient Sri Lanka with special reference to Bogoda', given to the 10th General Assembly of the ICOMOS International Wood Committee at Colombo in 1993. Lalchandra gives the bridge as 50 ft 10.75 in long and 3 ft 6 in wide, mounted on round wooden columns each 12 to 13 inches in diameter, with a pier of two wooden columns giving it strength at the centre of the span, and handrails on both sides. The roof, he notes, is built according to Sinhalese architectural practice, and the carvings on the rafters can be compared with the wood carving of the Embekke Devalaya and of the Magul Maduwa. The English and Sinhala Wikipedia articles give different figures — a span of about 15 m, a breadth of about 1.5 m and a roof about 2.4 m high — and a travel listing gives about 40 feet. The timbers named are kos or jack (Artocarpus heterophyllus) and kumbuk (Terminalia arjuna) for the structure, with kaluwara (Diospyros ebenum) and milla (Vitex pinnata) for the carved work; a 2016 Sinhala magazine article names five species, adding 'mil'. Sri Lanka Post put the bridge on a Rs 15 stamp in 2011, in a series on bridges and culverts.

The bridge belongs to the temple beside it, and the temple is very much older than any date proposed for the bridge. Two cave inscriptions in Early Brahmi script, dated on letter forms to between the third century BC and the first century AD, were published by Senarath Paranavitana in the first volume of Inscriptions of Ceylon in 1970. One of them reads 'Parumaka-Tisha-puta-Bamadatasha lene agata-anaga[ta]-catu-disha-shagasha paditite' — 'The cave of Brahmadatta, son of the chief Tissa, is established for the Sangha of the four quarters, present and absent.' The cave temple and the monks' dwelling both carry Kandyan-period architectural features. Inside the cave are three Buddha statues, reclining, seated and standing, the seated one under a makara torana made of wood; the ceiling carries floral decoration connected with the stupa and the relics, and the walls carry the Sat-satiya, the first seven weeks after the enlightenment, and episodes from the Jataka tales. Two further statues are identified, one probably as Ananda and one as Visnu, and a room at one end of the outer verandah is reserved for Visnu, Saman and Kataragama. The temple has no stupa at all, which Lalchandra records as a peculiarity, since a stupa is the one building a Buddhist temple is expected to have. A granite stone at the cave entrance carries the year 1929, probably for the extension of the verandah, and renovations are recorded in 2477 of the Buddhist era, 1933. The monks' dwelling is said to be between 250 and 350 years old and the eight circular pillars carrying its outer verandah roof are described as having features of Dutch architecture. A copper-plate inscription of Kirti Sri Rajasinha, who reigned from 1747 to 1781, granted on behalf of both this temple and the one at Passara, is held here. Behind the cave is a tunnel whose end is unknown; local tradition runs it to the temple at Dowa, to the Narangala hill and as far as Ruwanwella, and attaches the cave to Vattagamini Abhaya, King Valagamba, hiding from an invasion, in one telling for nearly three years, in a cave given to him by a regional ruler of the Uva country named Brahmadatta. The cave temple, the monks' dwelling and the wooden bridge are all declared archaeological protected monuments, by a gazette notification of 22 November 2002 and again by a gazette extraordinary of 1 June 2023.

The bridge is on an ancient footpath route linking Badulla and Kandy. The received account of why it exists is that it was built so that pilgrims walking from Badulla to worship the Tooth Relic at Kandy could cross a rock-strewn stream, and that the roof was added afterwards so that they had somewhere to rest out of the sun and the rain — which would make it a bridge and an ambalama, a wayside rest, at the same time. That reading is given as tradition rather than as anything documented. A folk tale is attached to its building: a father and a son built it, and the father, leaving the last portion of the work and its attendant rites to be done in his presence, told the son not to attempt them because he did not know them; the son, in a hurry to finish, did them himself, and because the work was not completed according to the rites a curse fell on him and he died untimely.

And then there is the age, which is where the record turns on itself. The single most repeated sentence about this bridge, carried verbatim by the English Wikipedia article, by the Sinhala one and by dozens of travel and heritage pages, is that it was built in the sixteenth century, during the Dambadeniya era. Dambadeniya was the capital from 1220 to 1272, and the dynasty seated there reigned until 1345; the sixteenth century is the fifteen hundreds. The sentence puts one bridge in two periods roughly three hundred years apart, and it cannot be right as it stands. Around it sit the others. 'Over 400 years old', in both Wikipedia articles. 'About 600 years ago or during the Kandyan Period', which is what lankapradeepa reports from Lalchandra 1993 and from Priyadarshani and Gunasena 2017, and which is itself loose, because six hundred years lands in the early fourteen hundreds, before the Kandyan kingdom. 'The 1600s'. Built by Kirti Sri Rajasinha, 1747 to 1782. A Dambadeniya-period original of about 1220 to 1283, brought to its present state by Sri Vikrama Rajasinha, the last king of Kandy, 1798 to 1815, who is credited with adding the railings, the planks and the tiled roof. 'Over 800 years old', in visitor reviews. Behind all of them there is only one kind of reason ever given, and it is stylistic: the bridge and the cave temple carry architectural features of the Kandyan period, and the carving on the rafter laths resembles Kandyan work. No inscription, chronicle entry, grant, radiocarbon date or tree-ring study for the bridge's own timber was found anywhere in this research. The Sinhala Wikipedia article has carried an unanswered request for a citation on 'the oldest wooden bridge in Sri Lanka' since September 2010, and another on 'the planks are said to have come from a single tree' since December 2011.

The last layer is what has been done to it since. One magazine account states that the kumbuk pillars were originally dug into the rock and that concrete was laid round them in 1986, with the permission of the Archaeological Department, to protect them from rocks coming down the stream in the monsoon. A travel listing states that the bridge now stands on concrete abutments which replaced the original wooden pillars resting on rock slabs. Another states that iron nails and concrete support beams were added by archaeologists in recent times. A heritage site states that the bridge was in severely deteriorated condition until a few years ago and has since been restored by the Department of Archaeology. None of these is sourced to a conservation report, they cannot all be true together, and between them they put a question mark over the one sentence that everybody repeats about this structure, which is that there is no metal and no other material anywhere in it.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C033 turns on a single word and this site is chosen for that word rather than for a resemblance. Both of the concept's sources say, plainly and early, that the six are not called roots because they cause a mind to arise; Pradeepika lists the actual conditions of arising separately so that the roots are left doing one job, and Margaya contrasts the Abhidhamma sense of the term with the everyday sense in which fire causes smoke. What a root does is hold. It fixes the mind and what travels with it firmly onto its object, the way a tree's roots keep the tree from falling — which is the sources' own image, not an illustration this film has supplied. A root, in this teaching, is what a state is standing on.

That definition asks for a structure, and it asks for a particular kind of structure. Most buildings answer the question 'what holds this up?' by pointing at a second material: stone under timber, iron in concrete, cable over a deck. This one cannot. The support and the supported are the same substance all the way through, and the fastening is the same substance again — pins of wood driven through wooden members, so that the joint between the holding and the held is not even a change of material. That is why this place and not another. The film does not have to argue that the holding is of a piece with the thing held; it can photograph a pin the size of a finger and let the frame carry it.

The record then does what no staging could. The question 'what made this?' has been asked of this bridge repeatedly for a century and has never been answered. Four centuries, six, eight; a thirteenth-century capital and a sixteenth-century date in the same sentence; a Kandyan king, or the last king of Kandy, or an unnamed builder in folklore with his son. Every proposal rests on how the carving looks. Meanwhile the answer to the other question — what is holding it up — has been available to everybody who ever crossed it, at ankle height, for the whole of that time. The two questions come apart here in the plainest possible way, and that separation is exactly the one C033 insists on: the sources refuse to let 'root' mean 'cause', and this is a place where the cause is genuinely lost and the support is genuinely visible. If the definition were merely verbal, the site would only illustrate it. Because the record has actually mislaid the origin, the site demonstrates that the second question does not depend on the first.

C008 does two jobs and the second is a restraint. It supplies the sentence C033's own digest says C033 lacks: delusion as a darkening that stops a matter being known as it is, present in all unwholesome minds and dominant in two — and those two are the one-rooted minds of C033's tables, the flat, neutral, unprompted states of doubt and restlessness. That is the film's sixth beat and it is spoken in the darkest frame the interior will give. But C008's digest also forbids the easy version of this film. The bridge's unsettled dating is not the doubt the sources warn about: Pradeepika expressly separates ordinary not-knowing about something one cannot yet investigate from the hindrance, and restricts the hindrance to eight named matters, none of which is the age of a building. So the film quotes the impossible sentence, says that nobody knows, and then refuses to diagnose the record. That refusal is the most honest thing in the film and it is also the thing that keeps the whole idea inside its sources.

What the film must not do follows from the same reading, and the location makes the temptation obvious. 'You cannot see what holds it up' is available here as a phrase and it would be false twice over: false about the bridge, where the posts and the pins are in plain sight, and false about the doctrine, which offers a classification of moments rather than a concealed mechanism to be uncovered. The film says what the structure is. It says what the sources mean by a root. It sets the two beside each other and stops. The only join it permits itself is the one the list itself makes: six items of one kind, three that hold a mind onto its object and three that hold it the other way, with Pradeepika's narrow claim that each of the second three undoes its own opposite. Nothing is brought in from outside — not into the bridge, and not into the argument.
what_is_certain: The bridge stands beside Bogoda Raja Maha Viharaya in Bogoda village, Grama Niladhari Division No. 76 of Bogoda, Haliela Divisional Secretary's Division, Badulla District, and crosses the Gallanda Oya, a tributary of the Mahaweli.

The ancient Len Viharaya, the Awasa-geya and the ancient wooden bridge in the temple premises are declared archaeological protected monuments by two gazette notifications: No. 1264 of 22 November 2002 and the Gazette Extraordinary No. 2334/41 of 1 June 2023, p.4A.

The one measured description located is M.D. Lalchandra's, in 'Bridges in ancient Sri Lanka with special reference to Bogoda', given to the 10th General Assembly of the ICOMOS International Wood Committee at Colombo in 1993, pp.41–51: 50 ft 10.75 in long, 3 ft 6 in wide, mounted on round wooden columns each 12 to 13 inches in diameter, with a pier of two wooden columns at the centre of the span, handrails on both sides, a roof built according to Sinhalese architectural practice, and rafter carvings comparable with the wood carving of the Embekke Devalaya and the Magul Maduwa. Reported here through lankapradeepa.com; the paper itself was not obtained.

The Department of Archaeology's Badulla district inventory is Priyadarshani, S.A.N. and Gunasena, I.P.P., 2017, Pauranika Sthana Ha Smaraka: Badulla Distrikkaya, ISBN 955-9159-48-8, with this site at pp.30–33.
The archaeological description states that all the components of the bridge, including the decking, the roof, the roof tiles, the balustrades and the nails, are made of wood.

The timber species named for the bridge are kos or jack (Artocarpus heterophyllus) and kumbuk (Terminalia arjuna) for the structure, and kaluwara (Diospyros ebenum) and milla (Vitex pinnata) for the carved and decorative work.
The roof is tiled with flat tiles, and the tiles and the rafter carving are attributed to Kandyan-period practice.

Two cave inscriptions in Early Brahmi script, dated on letter forms to between the third century BC and the first century AD, were published in Paranavitana, S., 1970, Inscriptions of Ceylon, Volume I, p.57. One reads 'Parumaka-Tisha-puta-Bamadatasha lene agata-anaga[ta]-catu-disha-shagasha paditite', translated there as 'The cave of Brahmadatta, son of the chief Tissa, is established for the Sangha of the four quarters, present and absent.'
A copper-plate inscription of King Kirti Sri Rajasinha (1747–1781), granted on behalf of both the Bogoda and the Passara viharas, is in the possession of this temple.

The cave temple holds three Buddha statues in reclining, seated and standing positions, the seated one under a wooden makara torana; the ceiling carries floral decoration linked with the stupa and the relics; the walls carry the Sat-satiya and episodes from the Jataka tales; and two further statues are identified, one probably as Ananda and one as the god Visnu. A separate room at one end of the outer verandah is reserved for Visnu, Saman and Kataragama.
The temple has no stupa, which Lalchandra records as a peculiarity.
A granite stone at the cave entrance carries a record of the year 1929, probably the date of the extension of the verandah, and renovations to the cave temple are recorded in 2477 B.E. (1933).
The Awasa-ge is said to be 250 to 350 years old, and the eight circular pillars supporting the roof of its outer verandah are described as having features of Dutch architecture.

The English Wikipedia article gives the span as nearly 15 m (49 ft) long and 1.5 m (4.9 ft) broad, with a tiled roof structure 2.4 m (7.9 ft) tall running its entire length; the Sinhala article gives the same three figures.
Sri Lanka Post issued a Rs 15 commemorative stamp showing the bridge in 2011, in a series on bridges and culverts.

Road access is from the Hali Ela junction on the Badulla–Bandarawela road: about 11 km on the Hali Ela–Welimada road to Jangulla junction, then left about 2.5 km, the road ending at the temple, with about a hundred steps down to the river. A second route via Meegahakiula and the Alugolla road, then the Kandegedara school road, is given as 23.3 km.
The OpenStreetMap node for the bridge gives 7.0079106 N, 80.9963053 E, in Bogoda, Jangulla, Badulla District, Uva Province.
Dambadeniya was the capital of the island from 1220 to 1272, and the dynasty seated there reigned until 1345. This is the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.
what_is_disputed: THE DATE, and the contradiction is the finding, not a nuisance to be tidied. The most repeated sentence about this bridge, carried verbatim by the English Wikipedia article, by the Sinhala Wikipedia article and by dozens of travel and heritage pages, is that it was 'built in the 16th century during the Dambadeniya era'. The sixteenth century is the fifteen hundreds. Dambadeniya was the capital from 1220 to 1272 and its dynasty ended in 1345 — the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. The sentence therefore assigns one structure to two periods about three hundred years apart, and it cannot be true as written. No source for it was found anywhere; it is reproduced, not argued. Which half of it anyone means is not recoverable from the sentence itself.

The rival datings, none of which this research can decide between: 'over 400 years old' (English and Sinhala Wikipedia); 'about 600 years ago or during the Kandyan Period' (reported from Lalchandra 1993 and Priyadarshani and Gunasena 2017), which is itself internally loose, since six hundred years before the present is the early fourteen hundreds and therefore before the Kandyan kingdom; 'believed to date back to the 1600s'; commissioned by King Kirti Sri Rajasinha (1747–1782); a Dambadeniya-period original of circa 1220–1283 brought to its present state by Sri Vikrama Rajasinha (1798–1815), who is credited with the railings, the wooden planks and the flat-tiled roof; and 'over 800 years old', which appears in visitor reviews. The span of the claims is roughly six hundred years wide.

What any of those dates rests on. Every dating located in this research is stylistic: the bridge and the cave temple carry architectural features of the Kandyan period, and the rafter carving resembles Kandyan work. No inscription, chronicle entry, land grant, radiocarbon determination or dendrochronological study of the bridge's own timber was found. The honest answer to 'how old is it' is that nobody consulted here knows, and the reason is not that the answer is hidden but that the work has not been done or has not been published where it can be read.

'The oldest surviving wooden bridge in Sri Lanka.' Attributed to archaeologists in several accounts and repeated everywhere. The Sinhala Wikipedia article has carried an unanswered citation-needed tag on this claim since September 2010. The narrower claim that it is the only surviving wooden bridge of its kind from its era is made by the archaeological sources and is better supported. A 2016 Sinhala magazine article escalates it to the first bridge in the world made entirely of wood, which nothing supports.

'The planks are said to have come from a single tree.' Repeated in both Wikipedia articles and across travel writing; carries an unanswered citation-needed tag on the Sinhala article dated December 2011. It also sits badly beside the same sources' own species list, which names jack and kumbuk for the structure and kaluwara and milla for the carving, and beside the Sinhala magazine account which names five species.

Whether the structure is still entirely timber, which is the claim the film's own argument leans on and therefore the one that has to be checked hardest. A magazine account states that the kumbuk pillars were originally dug into the rock and that concrete was laid in 1986, with the permission of the Archaeological Department, to protect the pillars from rocks cascading down the stream in the monsoon. A travel listing states that the bridge 'stands on concrete abutments, replacing the original wooden pillars resting on rock slabs'. Another states that iron nails and concrete support beams were added by archaeologists in recent times. A heritage site states that the bridge was in severely deteriorated condition until a few years ago and has since been restored by the Department of Archaeology. None of these is sourced to a conservation report, they cannot all be true simultaneously, and none is compatible with Lalchandra's description of round wooden columns 12 to 13 inches in diameter with a two-column pier. What is actually timber and what is not has to be established on site.

The dimensions. 50 ft 10.75 in long by 3 ft 6 in wide (Lalchandra 1993); about 15 m by 1.5 m (both Wikipedia articles); 'approximately 40 feet' (a travel listing). The roof is given as 2.4 m or about 8 feet high. The figure of 6 feet in width, which is in circulation, is supported by neither of the measured accounts.

What the span rests on, where the accounts contradict each other and in one case themselves. Lalchandra gives round wooden columns of 12 to 13 inches diameter with a pier of two wooden columns at the centre. Both Wikipedia articles say the structure stands on a huge tree trunk 11 m in height. A 2016 Sinhala article says it stands on a kumbuk trunk about 30 feet tall, then says three large timber trunks laid across the stream were used to build it, then a few lines later says the bridge rests on two large timber trunks. An English account gives eleven carved pillars supporting the roof.

A first restoration by the Department of Archaeology in 1963–64. This appeared in a search summary attributed to the Sinhala Wikipedia article; it is not present in that article's text as read here, and no source for it was located. It is not used.

The route and the purpose. That the bridge lies on an ancient footpath route linking Badulla and Kandy is stated in the reference literature. That it was built so that pilgrims from Badulla could cross the stream on their way to worship the Tooth Relic at Kandy, and that the roof was added later so that they could rest out of the sun and rain, is given as folklore. Its double function as an ambalama, a wayside rest, is described as 'thought' rather than established.

The name of the stream. Every archaeological source and both Wikipedia articles give the Gallanda Oya. One travel listing puts the bridge over the Loggal Oya, which is a different stream in the same district. The archaeological reading is preferred and the discrepancy is recorded.

The temple's own traditions: that the cave was given to Vattagamini Abhaya, King Valagamba, by a regional ruler of the Uva country named Brahmadatta; that the king hid there for something like three years during an invasion; and that the tunnel behind the cave once ran to the temple at Dowa, to the Narangala hill and to Ruwanwella. These are recorded as tradition and folklore. The Brahmi inscription does name a Brahmadatta, son of the chief Tissa, which is presumably what the tradition has attached itself to, and it establishes nothing else in the story. The tunnel is said not to be fully visible today.

The folk tale of the bridge's building: that a father and son built it, that the father forbade the son to perform the final portion of the work and its rites in his absence, that the son did so anyway in his haste, and that a curse fell on him for a bridge not completed according to the rites and he died untimely. Folklore, recorded here as folklore. The film does not narrate it, both because it cannot be sourced and because it is a death the series has no business dramatising.

The distance from Badulla, which is given inconsistently everywhere: 7 km west (English Wikipedia), 13 km south (Sinhala Wikipedia and much travel writing), 10 km, 11 km from the Hali Ela junction, 15 km from Ella. The coordinates put the site roughly 7 km west-north-west of Badulla in a straight line, so the larger figures are road distances by different routes and the directions given with them do not agree.

unknowns: Nothing has been verified on the ground. No permission has been sought from the Department of Archaeology or from the temple, and a protected timber monument in daily use may well not be filmable on the terms this idea assumes.

Whether the structure is still entirely timber. Several accounts say concrete was laid round the posts in 1986 and that iron nails, concrete beams or concrete abutments have since been added; none is sourced to a conservation report. Beats 3, 4 and 7 depend on knowing which is true.

Whether the interior can be exposed on available light at any hour, and whether the bars of light through the tile gaps described here are actually there. No artificial light is permitted, so this decides the film.
Whether a wooden pin is visible anywhere on the structure at macro range. It is the payoff shot and no photograph of one was found.
Whether the joints, the posts and the underside can be framed from the bank and the stream bed without anyone getting onto or under the structure.
Whether the site can be scheduled so that no child is on the span while the camera rolls. It is a village footpath to a temple.

The three printed works the site description rests on — Lalchandra 1993, Paranavitana 1970, Priyadarshani and Gunasena 2017 — were not obtained, so every measurement and every dating attributed to them here is at one remove.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified; the printed sources behind its measurements and datings were not read. No scene or shot is decided here.
